Shoshone

Shoshone is a broad name for distinct regional peoples and communities, not one single government or uniform history. This reviewed introduction centers publicly documented histories connected to Idaho, including the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes at Fort Hall and the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of Duck Valley, while also placing Eastern and Northwestern Shoshone sources in view. It is a selected reading guide, not an exhaustive account of all Shoshone communities.

A source guide for a deeper dive.This entry provides a brief orientation and an organized reading path. A comprehensive deep dive has not yet been completed. Follow the annotated sources and distinguish primary community accounts from outside reference material.
Still unfinished

Twelve distinct substantive works have actual-content inspection records: community publications from Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Eastern Shoshone and the Northwestern Band; a community–NPS exhibit; two place-based NPS histories; a Northwestern Shoshone historian’s selected chapter pages; a cited Wyoming history article; primary treaty and constitutional texts; and a federal Duck Valley water-settlement statement. These support a carefully scoped introduction across several regional communities, but the entry is a broad umbrella and evidence depth remains uneven. Reaching the source target does not make the collection complete or community-reviewed.

Assessment recorded October 23, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • The entry’s broad “Shoshone” access point cannot stand in for separate studies of the many Shoshone governments, communities, bands, and family histories. The current sample is uneven across Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Wind River, the Northwestern Band, and other Shoshone communities.
  • More community-authored histories, language materials, and contemporary accounts from Shoshone governments in Nevada, Utah, Idaho, and Wyoming remain to be inspected; no single source represents all communities.
  • The Fort Bridger Treaty text, the Shoshone-Bannock Treaty Day account, and WyoHistory describe the separate Bannock reservation and later move using different chronology. The relationship between reservation promises, relocation, and later Fort Hall governance needs further original-record review.
  • Mae Parry’s 2000 chapter was reviewed at selected pages only. Its family and oral-history evidence is attributed, while its historical interpretations are not treated as universal community consensus.
  • The Shoshone-Paiute cultural page and Eastern Shoshone About page contain undated or broad totals and historical claims that require independent checking; no current population, acreage, or deep-time claim is reused.
  • The Shoshone-Bannock and Shoshone-Paiute language evidence here is introductory. Comparative specialist work on Shoshone varieties, Bannock, and Northern Paiute, with each community’s terminology and stewardship preferences, remains needed.
  • No community review or endorsement is recorded. No historical map was independently inspected for this batch and none has been newly assigned.
01

Names, communities, and scope

“Shoshone” is used for related peoples whose histories span a large area of the inland West; the name does not identify one government or one community. The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes describe their Fort Hall government as comprising Northern Shoshone and Bannock bands, while their account distinguishes the peoples’ languages. The Shoshone-Paiute Tribes’ Duck Valley history describes a separate community formed from Western Shoshone and Northern Paiute bands whose reservation crosses today’s Idaho–Nevada border. The Eastern Shoshone Tribe and Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation are distinct governments with their own public historical accounts. The NPS wayside exhibit’s term “Newenee” and its “Shoshonean” language grouping belong to a specific Shoshone-Bannock collaboration and should not be treated as universal names for every Shoshone community.

02

Idaho homelands and seasonal movement

For the Fort Hall community, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes describe ancestral lands extending beyond present reservation and state borders, and document seasonal use of southern Idaho’s river, camas, salmon, and high-country areas. The National Park Service’s Craters of the Moon account outlines a seasonal round through Fort Hall, Camas Prairie, the Boise and Snake Rivers, and hunting areas farther north and east. That is a place-based NPS interpretation, not a complete account of all Shoshone families or a present-day territorial boundary. Northwestern Shoshone historian Mae Parry’s chapter separately describes seasonal gathering and travel in northern Utah, southern Idaho, and adjoining regions; her account helps show why present state lines and reservation maps cannot stand in for community history.

Read the sources [1] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes [5] National Park Service [11] WyoHistory.org; Wyoming State Historical Society

03

Language, cultural work, and public knowledge

The Shoshone-Bannock Language and Cultural Preservation Department describes teaching both Shoshone and Bannock, maintaining archives and family-history materials, recording oral histories, and protecting information it considers confidential or sensitive. The NPS Newenee exhibit was prepared with Shoshone-Bannock representatives and includes artwork by Shoshone-Bannock artist Derek No-Sun Brown; its welcome and language examples should be read as a specific community contribution to a public park exhibit. These sources document programs and public interpretation, not language-use totals or outcomes. This guide does not reproduce restricted material.

Read the sources [3] Shoshone-Bannock Tribes Language and Cultural Preservation Department [4] National Park Service, with Shoshone-Bannock Tribes representatives

04

Treaties, reservation formation, and distinct governments

The 1868 Fort Bridger treaty names the Eastern Shoshone and Bannock parties separately. Its text set aside the Wind River reservation for named Shoshone signatories and promised a later reservation for the Bannacks in the Portneuf and “Kansas Prairie” countries. The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes’ Treaty Day account says the separate Bannock reservation was never established and that Bannock people were relocated to Fort Hall in 1869. WyoHistory’s timeline describes later Bannock moves in 1873 and the arrival of Pocatello’s band in 1876. These accounts differ in how they date the move and do not make the treaty’s promise identical to its later implementation. The Fort Hall Constitution and Bylaws, approved in 1936 and amended through 2013 in the published copy, describe that government’s own jurisdiction and council structure; they should not be generalized to other Shoshone governments.

Read the sources [7] U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Secretary [8] Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, 1868; compiled by Charles J. 05

Duck Valley and Shoshone-Paiute history

The Shoshone-Paiute Tribes’ cultural department locates Duck Valley across Idaho and Nevada and describes the community as including Western Shoshone and Northern Paiute bands. Its historical account covers executive orders, movement on and off the reservation, resistance to a proposed relocation to Fort Hall, the 1936 constitution, and schooling. The page’s acreage and membership figures are undated and are not repeated here. A 2021 Department of the Interior statement for the record explains the Duck Valley water-rights settlement and the federal trust funds for irrigation infrastructure; it is a narrow legal and administrative source, not a full account of the Tribes’ history or water knowledge.

Read the sources [6] Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of the Duck Valley Indian Reservation [7] U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Secretary

06

Northwestern and Eastern Shoshone histories

Mae Parry’s chapter, written by a Northwestern Shoshone historian for a Utah history volume proposed by Utah Indian leaders, combines family oral history, written records, and tribal history. The selected pages discuss the Bear River Massacre of 1863, survivors’ accounts, the settlement of Washakie, testimony about homes burned in 1960, and the Northwestern Band’s later legal history. Utah Humanities’ 2024 account, produced for the Northwestern Band, describes Mae Parry’s archival and oral-history work and continuing community efforts. These sources provide Northwestern-specific context; their accounts do not represent every Shoshone community. The Eastern Shoshone government’s About page is also retained as its own public account, while its deep-time and treaty-area figures are left unattributed in the synthesis because they need closer comparison with community and archaeological sources.

Read the sources [10] Eastern Shoshone Tribe [11] WyoHistory.org; Wyoming State Historical Society [12] Mae Parry; edited by Forrest S. Cuch; Utah State Division of Indian Affairs and Utah State Division of History, 2000

07

What this collection can and cannot establish

This source set supports an introductory comparison of several living Shoshone communities and particular treaty, language, place, and government records. Its coverage remains uneven: Fort Hall, Duck Valley, Wind River, and the Northwestern Band have different kinds and depths of documentation here, while many other Shoshone communities, family histories, languages, and contemporary priorities are not represented. Some historical sources use old collective labels or compress distinct bands into one timeline. The collection has twelve substantive works with actual content inspected, but that count is separate from adequacy, completeness, or community review. No community endorsement is recorded, no population total is offered, and no map is assigned by geographic inference.

The Northwestern Shoshone — A History of Utah’s American Indians ↗

Read selected pages of Mae Parry’s 48-page chapter in the digitized book viewer: pp. 25–26 on regional seasonal life; pp. 34–42 on the Bear River Massacre and survivor accounts; pp. 59–61 on Washakie testimony; and pp. 69–72 on the Box Elder treaty and Northwestern Band legal history. The book introduction identifies this as a Utah Indian leaders’ project; Parry’s family and oral-history sources are attributed as such. This selected-page review is not a reading of every page in the chapter.
